sentences.text: Rajasaurus was a robust predatory dinosaur from India, estimated to measure approximately 6.6 meters in length.
Its body stood about 2.4 meters tall and weighed between 400 and 700 kilograms.
This species is distinguished by a single horn on its forehead, elongated supratemporal fenestrae, and iliac crests separating the brevis platform from the hip joint.
The fossil site of Rajasaurus in Balasinor is known as the "Jurassic Park of India" due to its popularity with tourists.
Rajasaurus appears in the Prehistoric Planet episode "Badlands," hunting Isisaurus hatchlings in the Deccan Traps.
The genus Rajasaurus was named by Wilson and colleagues in 2003 after fossil bones were discovered between 1982 and 1984 by Suresh Srivastava of the Geological Survey of India.

The 2003 description of Rajasaurus was based on a partial skeleton including the braincase, spine, hip, legs, and tail, marking the first time such post-cranial remains were preserved for an Indian theropod.

Fossils of Rajasaurus were found in the Lameta Formation in Gujarat, Western India, a site first discovered in 1981 by geologists G. N. Dwivedi and Dhananjay Mahendrakumar Mohabey of the Geological Survey of India.
Rajasaurus was likely an ambush predator, similar to other abelisaurids, which may have hunted large prey using an ambush and bite-and-hold strategy.
It likely had a bite force of approximately 3500 Newtons, similar to Allosaurus.

Researchers suggest the horn of Rajasaurus may have been used for display or head-butting, though the lack of spongy bone in the skull suggests head-butting involved low-momentum pushes like marine iguanas or focused strikes on the neck and flank like giraffes.
Comparatively short leg bones suggest Rajasaurus was slower than similar-sized theropods.
In 2003, Wilson classified Rajasaurus in the subfamily Carnotaurinae, a grouping that demonstrates the widespread global distribution of this group of dinosaurs.
In 2014, paleontologist Thierry Tortosa established the subfamily Majungasaurinae to group Rajasaurus with other abelisaurids based on elongated antorbital fenestrae and a triangular sagittal crest.
Rajasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, approximately 66 million years ago, in what is now the Indian Subcontinent.
Rajasaurus closely resembled the abelisaurid Majungasaurus from Madagascar, despite a time separation of 20 million years.
It is debated whether Rajasaurus, Lametasaurus, and Indosaurus are synonymous species, though this remains unconfirmed due to fragmentary remains and the loss of the Lametasaurus specimen.
Hypotheses suggest abelisaurid migration between Europe and India occurred via Africa or through island-hopping along the Dras-Kohistan volcanic arc, though these explanations remain questionable.
